utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technicians, the interpreters; good morning, members of the registry, counsel for the Prosecution, Defence; good morning, General Krstic. We are now going to resume our work by bringing in our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Hadzihasanovic. Let me remind you that you're still under an oath. You may be seated. We are now going to continue with your testimony. General, we were still at the narrative part of your testimony. I hope that the documents were properly marked for identification yesterday and that that problem has been taken care of. So I think that you may continue.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Your Honours. Yesterday in my statement I wanted to give you an idea of what the 28th Division looked like, what its strength was, its weaponry, and its combat readiness. So I don't think there's anything particular to add to what I stated yesterday concerning that issue, unless you have certain questions. But I think that you asked me yesterday two questions, that is, what I knew about the attack against Srebrenica and the structure of the column that was moving after the attack towards Tuzla. So if I understand Your Honour's questions correctly, I should like to begin with answering them. I personally was not a participant in those events in Srebrenica. I was not present there and I was not in the column which was moving out of it, so my testimony about it is based on what I was able to learn as a member who was -- as a Chief of Staff of the BH army, whether I learnt it through written documentation or through my contacts with the people. On the 6th of July, 1995, I was actually there on the spot when the column moved out, so I was able to have contact with those people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the date?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had a task, with a group of other people, to receive the members of the column and to see what had happened with the members of the 28th Division. According to my knowledge, the attack, the intense attack on Srebrenica started on the 6th of July from the southern side of Srebrenica, from the direction of Zeleni Jadar, Pribicevac, Zalazje and Zvijezda villages. I also know that it was there that the Serb forces started their first offensive activities towards Srebrenica; that is, they started moving towards north. The front line was pierced there, and the division command requested the UN forces to try and inform all relevant factors of those attacks, and also, of course, to try and prevent them. That was done in various ways, through a certain period of time, and I cannot give you any detailed information about that, but I know that there were negotiations to that effect. And I know that initially, at the first time of the attack, the UN forces had to abandon some of their observation posts. On the 6th of July, they abandoned the first of their observations posts. And finally, I think that they had to withdraw from a total of three OPs. So the command of the 28th Division was informed that the UN forces stationed in Srebrenica had asked for assistance and also had asked for NATO strikes, that is, that the southern part of the enclave had to be abandoned by the BH army because of the attacks. They were actually told that the targets would not be selected in order to try and stop the attack, and that is why the BH army abandoned those positions. But as they were expecting those strikes, and I believe there was only one such strike by air force, nothing of any significance happened, and the Serb forces continued their attack towards Srebrenica. The BH army units withdrew to the hills around Srebrenica, and on about the 10th of July, they started gathering, the population started gathering in the villages north of Srebrenica and also the elements of the army started assembling there. I know that on the 11th of July, almost all members of the army gathered in the village of Susnjari. In addition to the military, as far as I know and according to the information that I have, there were about 7.000 civilians in that village. There was a very small number of women there, not more than ten, I think. So on the 11th of July, in the evening, the division command, together with the municipal authorities, on their own initiative decided to move in a column and try and leave the area of the protected zone in the direction of the free territory around Tuzla. I think that that decision was taken around 2200 hours on the 11th of July. According to the statement by the late Chief of Staff with whom I had an opportunity to talk, Mr. Becirovic, I think that was his name, the column consisted between 12.000 and 15.000 people and almost the complete composition, the complete division was there, that is, 5.500 to 6.000 troops. It was decided that the column should go along the axis Konjevic Polje-Bratunac moving along the ridges west of that axis, and that the asphalt road be crossed over in the area between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba and that they should continue towards Tuzla after crossing the tarmac on that spot. The length of the column, according to the information that I have, was between 12 and 15 kilometres, and the time span was about two and a half hours from the head and the tail of the column. They started on the 11th of July around midnight. As far as I could note, it was structured as follows: The head of the column consisted of elements of the 284th Brigade who were followed by the 280th Brigade and I know that the Chief of Staff told me that he was amongst the members of that unit. Then followed civilians together with the military, and the last element of the column was the independent battalion which was also part of the 28th Division. Before they reached the asphalt road at Konjevic Polje towards Vlasenica, an artillery attack was launched against the second half of the column. Fire was opened from various kinds of artillery weapons on the tail of the column, and the head of the column realised that there was nobody on the tarmac road. They had started crossing the road on that spot, not knowing that the second half of the column was, in the meantime, exposed to a fierce attack, artillery attack. That was on the 12th of July. I think that about 80 or 100 people managed to cross the tarmac road, that is one-third of the column. After that, some APCs and a tank, I believe, arrived and the Serb forces pierced the column on that spot. So the first third of the column managed to cross the asphalt road, and they were waiting to see what would happen with the rest of the column. However, throughout that day, the second half of the column was exposed to heavy shooting and shelling, and during the night, they probably thought that other members of the column would also cross the road, but nobody did so they decided to move on. I know that because the Chief of Staff who told me about this was with that portion of the column. They continued towards the Udrc mount where they assembled, and at that point in time they sent a group of people back to the asphalt road to wait and see whether anybody else would cross over, but they had to return because no one was crossing the road any more. So on the 13th of July, they continued on their way across the Udrc mount in the direction of Kalesija that is towards the Kalesija-Zvornik asphalt road. On that part of the road, they were ambushed on several occasions. There were fatalities and casualties there, and on the 14th of July or the 15th, they reached the area of the village of Medzedza, that is the area of Crni Vrh, which is a hill near Kalesija. On the 15th of July, they tried to leave the area of Crni Vrh and the wider area is called Parlog. They tried to move closer to the front lines but they were ambushed again so they had to go back and they spent the night there. In the afternoon hours of the 15th of July, they selected a large group of people who then fought with the Serbs at one point in time, but they were unable to do anything. So on the 15th of July in the evening hours, they went back to the same spot to spend the night. On the 16th of July, in a similar way with a group of people, they attempted once again a breakthrough and at that point in time, the communication was established with the front line through a walkie-talkie so the Corps Command, at that time, was already familiar with the spot where they could be expected to come out. In the early morning hours of the 16th of July, the front line was finally pierced by the elements of the 24th Division and the 212th Brigade. As for the other side, they were moving from the rear of the front and they managed to pierce the line along the distance of one and a half kilometres, and the civilians and the military which was with that group started entering the free area at that spot. However, as regards the asphalt road between Konjevic Polje and Vlasenica, in that area, there were very few people left, only an individual here and there who managed to go through. Later on, people who survived and who managed to come out told us that it was like a manhunt in that area near the asphalt road coming from Srebrenica going towards Kravica, Konjevic Polje, and then further on from Konjevic Polje towards Vlasenica near Kasaba. So that region was the theatre of a fierce manhunt, and I know that they were collecting people at three locations. One of them was the stadium near Nova Kasaba. The second one was a farm, agricultural farm in the village of Kravica. The third location was an elementary school or part of a factory in Kravica. And from those locations, according to what people said, they were taken towards Zvornik, and nothing was ever heard of them after that. After the 28th Division managed to pull out, elements of it, that is, we received them in the area of Tuzla. I know for sure that they were received on the following localities. After they had come out of the front line, the division command was received in the old mining institute in Tuzla. The 281st Brigade was assembled in the elementary school in the village of Basigovci. The 222nd Brigade was also assembled in the elementary school in the Vukovije village. The 223rd Brigade and the Independent Battalion was assembled in the village of Zivinice in the elementary school, and the 284th Brigade was assembled in the area of Ciljuge, where there were some hangars belonging to the former JNA. So that was their point of assembly. As regards other people from Srebrenica, I know that when the decision was reached on the 11th of July to leave the area of Srebrenica and to go towards Tuzla, that all other civilians - women, children, and the elderly - that on that same evening, and perhaps several days prior to that, that they were assembling in the UN base in Potocari. According to that information, there were about 30.000 people gathered in that area. The first information about these events in Srebrenica reached us only when the first trucks carrying women and children appeared in the area of Kladanj, the people who were transported from Potocari. They told us that there were cases of mistreatment and killing in the immediate vicinity of Potocari, and I believe that the Court has heard evidence of the eyewitnesses to those events. I don't want to go into those details, but I know that such incidents were common there at that time. The first review of troops took place on the 25th of July, 1995, and after that review, we managed to establish that 2.080 members of the 28th Division managed to pierce the front lines, and it was our assumption that there were probably several other members of the 28th Division who had gone to the village of Ciljuge, where there was a very big settlement organised for the civilian population who managed to get out. Those members of the division had probably gone to Tuzla to look for the members of their family. So we continued collating the information, to the extent it was possible, and on the 4th of August, 1995, or thereabouts, we managed to establish the accurate number of the members of the 28th Division who managed to get through. The number was 3.175. We also established that the number of individuals who were killed in the column was between 8.300 and 9.722. At that time the information we received was not consistent, but that was the approximate figure that we managed to establish. One can claim for certainty that 2.628 members, both soldiers and commanding officers, members of the 28th Division, were killed. When the decision was made for a breakthrough, we lost all connection with the column and the command of the division. They just told us, "We are starting. We're on the move towards Tuzla." And "towards Tuzla" is a very broad area, so we didn't know the actual direction. That is when our links with the 28th Division were severed, and we were to establish contact on the 15th, in the afternoon hours, and on the morning of the 16th, when they were near the front line at Crni Vrh. As to the structure of the column and the way in which they broke through, that is what I know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Hadzihasanovic. I think that you passed -- that you covered the points that we're interested in. I am now going to give the floor to the two parties; that is to say, I'm going to ask them if they want to take the floor. Mr. Harmon, do you have any questions for your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. General Hadzihasanovic, good morning. If the witness could be provided with Prosecution Exhibits 898 through 904.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, we're going to start with an exhibit that is marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 904, and as soon as you get it, I'm going to ask you to read it, to take a look at it to see if you're familiar with it, and then I'm going to ask you for your comments about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, are we starting with 904? Could you place the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, the reason I ask you about this particular document is you touched upon the materiel that was available and the manpower that was available to the 28th Division within the enclave. And I'd like you to first of all take a look at this document, which is a situation report from the 28th Division command, dated the 30th of June, 1995. It has been authored by Major Ramiz Becirovic, who was standing in for the commander and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the 28th Division sent to the command of the 2nd Corps, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can see that it was indeed signed by Ramiz Becirovic. I have not seen this document before. Quite obviously, it was not sent to the headquarters of the Supreme Command. But may I take a few moments to read through the document? Yes, this is a report, a situation report, dealing with some activities of the 28th Division, and it is sending out information where and when events occurred, as far as I can see from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you comment, General, about the contents of this document to the extent that you could touch upon, briefly, any activities that were of a nature where the 28th Division troops were going into territory that was occupied by the VRS in conducting operations. I don't want a long exposition on it, but can you touch briefly on that subject, to the extent that you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the army of the 28th Division would undertake any combat activities, because everything that we did in these parts, and the instructions we gave to the 2nd Corps, for the most part referred to the other units and did not apply to Srebrenica and Zepa. Therefore, the instructions -- we did not send out instructions from the Main Staff for things of this kind to be undertaken. Possibly it was something of a local character, an order issued locally perhaps, but we never defined precisely that if the 2nd Corps were to undertake any activities, that it should be done in Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least, as far as I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, General, just based on this document, is there any reason to dispute the content and the substance of this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of the document I cannot dispute because the document was written by the Chief of Staff and signed. So I suppose he wrote the truth. I personally do not know about these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn my attention now to another set of documents, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be provided with the remaining documents, please. That would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 898 through Prosecutor's Exhibit 903.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And while these documents are being distributed, General, the Court has heard evidence about a document. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 425. I'm sure you have not seen this document, but -- so I will acquaint you with parts of this document. It is a directive for further operations, Operation 7. It is dated March 8th, 1995, from the Supreme Command of the VRS. It is a lengthy document and it is signed by the Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. I'm not going to have you review it, I'm just going to summarise it for you. I'm going to read a part of -- two parts of this document. The first dealt with combat operations, and a part of the document that was directed to the Drina Corps includes the following sentence, "By planned and well thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, document in a later section under a title, "Support for Command Operations," a subpart entitled "Moral and Psychological Support," I'll read you a paragraph from this particular document. "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while, at the same time, avoiding condemnation of the International Community and international public opinion." Now, General, this is a document that's dated the 8th of March 1995. I raise this because, in your testimony yesterday, you said something to this effect: "By the end of 1994, the situation for the people was complex. All humanitarian aid or all humanitarian convoys had been blocked." Now, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you, if I could, and if we could put Prosecutor's Exhibit 898 on the ELMO and, General, do you have the B/C/S version 898 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this -- I'm going to show you 898 through Prosecutor's Exhibit 903, which are a succession of documents that were issued by the 28th Division. They are situation reports. They have all been authored by Ramiz Becirovic, and let me direct your attention, in this particular document, at this time, to the section dealing with humanitarian situation. Could you read that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that, in this particular document it says, that the humanitarian situation is extremely hard, and Ramiz Becirovic is requesting that constant efforts be made to deblock the humanitarian corridor to Srebrenica and enable the regular distribution of food, supplies to the local population. Now, could you turn to the next document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 899, and I'd like to direct your attention, General, to the last paragraph, number 4, entitled "The Humanitarian Situation." And this is a document 899, I'm sorry, that's dated the 6th of July. Let me read you this part of the document, General: "The situation continues to be extremely difficult. The food convoy announced for today has not arrived. Elderly and weak persons are in an exceptionally difficult situation due to starvation. The first people to die of hunger in Srebrenica after the demilitarisation were registered today. I request that every effort be made to deliver food to our area." Now, General, I'm just going to take you through these series of documents. If we could turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 900, which is the next document dated the 7th of July, again a document from the 28th Division and, again, from Major Ramiz Becirovic. I'd like to direct your attention to the last part of the document, dealing with the humanitarian situation. Let me read from this: "The humanitarian situation is worrying. Today more civilians have been registered as having died from hunger, and if significant quantities of food are not quickly brought in swiftly to the area, the course of events in the entire safe area is extremely uncertain." I won't read the rest of that particular document. If we could turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 901, which is another document issued by Ramiz Becirovic, this day, the following day, the 8th of July. And if we could turn to the last section of the document, General, "Humanitarian Situation," and I'll read parts of it. "This situation is also dramatic and practically hopeless. The civilian population is dying of hunger, and in a few days time the army will not have any food on the front lines." It goes on to say: "Even if we succeed in withstanding the military pressure we will very soon be forced to abandon this area because of a lack of food." Let me, General, turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 902, another report prepared by Ramiz Becirovic, this time dated the 9th of July. I'm going to read to you the report sent, a portion of that report sent by Mr. Becirovic dealing with the humanitarian situation. "The humanitarian situation is catastrophic. The population and soldiers have no food reserves and from tomorrow it will not be possible to supply the defence lines with food articles." And he pleads then for an effort to get the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. International Community engaged. Now, General, in respect of these documents that I have read to you, and in respect of your testimony yesterday that by the end of 1994, the situation for the people was complex, and in light of the document that I read to you from Dr. Karadzic from March of 1995, can you comment on these documents that I have shown you and informed you about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. But, Mr. President, I would do this in the following way; what I am going to say now I was going to say at the end of my presentation, at the end, but never mind, I can say it now. May I use a piece of paper that I have prepared in order to give an answer to the question that has been posed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following: Srebrenica was the final act of an overall scenario when it came to the Podrinje area and the task of the Drina Corps. I say this because it emerges from the following: The way in which that final act was realised, was implemented of this scenario, is the kind that you have read out. Because the ultimate goal was to do away with all the non-Serb population in the Drina River belt and that the non-Serbian population must disappear from those parts so that the Drina should no longer be a border between the states, the Serb states. I say this because I know that the assembly of Republika Srpska on the 12th or the 15th of May, I'm not quite sure, 1992, adopted its strategic goals where that was stated. That goal, under point 3, was implemented by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I know what your objection is going to be, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, unfortunately, I must say that the witness is overstepping the frameworks of the question and the topic that we are discussing today. And as I can see, he has a prepared document and is using it for that purpose. So my objection is to his answer, first of all, and, secondly, the use of any prepared document in doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the circumstances why this column left is important. I asked the witness questions about events and circumstances that led up to their departure. He commented on this in his direct examination, or his examination, his statement to the Chamber. I'm not aware of any documents that this witness may have or has prepared. I don't know what it is. It may be documents that are already in evidence, as far as I know. Until I can see what the document is, I'm not in a position to comment on whether he should or shouldn't show it or whether he can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we spent a lot of time discussing the importance of the region of Podrinje, and I'm sure you will recall that General Radinovic spoke at length about that issue. I think it is important for us to be able to gain a full understanding and it is precisely because of that that the Chamber summoned this witness to gain an overall view of the occurrences around Srebrenica. With respect to the document the General used, we said previously, we heard previously that the General was using notes. If he has a prepared document, he can place it on the ELMO, of course, and we can all see it. But if it's just a sort of aide-memoire for him, notes that he has compiled himself, it is legitimate for him to use them unless the parties would like to take a look at those documents. General, the document that you are reading from, is it an aide-memoire or is it a pre-compiled declaration?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an official document. This is a piece of paper on which I jotted down some things so as not to make a mistake. I quoted -- I wrote down the exact words and sentences of a document which is an original document, and that is the piece of paper that I'm now using. I have written down the exact words of that other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood, the witness wishes to read out a note he has made but which, in fact, is the text of another document. Then we have a problem again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Hadzihasanovic, to avoid any speculation, would you try to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecutor directly, please. Then we will have no need to debate this point. I'm going to ask Mr. Harmon to rephrase his question or state his question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I had asked you to comment on the materials that I had shown, and you were going to comment on that using some notes that you had prepared, and I take it you wanted to reference certain events or certain details that would support your comments. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you are correct, yes. I did not bring a document with me for me to say precisely what is written down in a document, without saying it in my own words. I made a note of that, and that is what I prepared. But if you don't wish me to read it out, if that is a point that is being contested, then I can paraphrase it, say it in my own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General. Tell us in your own words. I think that if we can avoid -- we will be able to avoid difficulties if you say it in your own words, please, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I wish to assist the Trial Chamber, and that is what I'm going to do. You asked me the question about the methodology of work in that area, in those parts, and the orders that were issued to the Drina Corps - amongst others, the prevention of humanitarian aid - all methods were resorted to for the Drina Corps to be able to complete the assignment it had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, can we hear the end of what the General is saying? But go ahead, as you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I understood, the General says that he was asked a question. I don't see that Mr. Harmon has actually asked him that question. He seems to be answering another question now, a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question asked by Mr. Harmon - and Mr. Harmon will put me right if I'm wrong - is, to my mind, that he showed the General a whole series of documents speaking about humanitarian aid. As you know, the General was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Bosnian army, and Mr. Harmon asked to hear a comment. He asked for his comment with respect to the humanitarian situation. He was asked to give his opinion and his point of view. Is that correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, General -- there, Mr. Visnjic, the General was answering that question. I think he grasped the meaning of the question and undertook to answer it. General, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand the question. Let me begin again. In view of the task assigned to the Drina Corps, and I know about that task, that assignment. The assignment was to eliminate the Drina River as a border between the Serb states, and the whole belt along the Drina River valley, and all the corps of the army of Republika Srpska had the task of making a delineation with respect to the other two peoples. So in addition to military activity, they resorted to other ways and means as well, amongst others, to prevent humanitarian aid and assistance, and this was confirmed in the document of General Mladic. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, and that is the testimonies that this Chamber has heard in respect of the shelling of the town of Srebrenica in civilian areas. I'm going to first of all read to you two testimonies of Defence witnesses in this trial. The first is a testimony of a Witness DC, a protected witness, and my colleague, Mr. Petrusic, asked the following question, and I'll only read part of it, part of the question. It's found at page 7441. I'm quoting from line 19 and I'm going over to the following page, line 5. My colleague, Mr. Petrusic, asked the following question of Witness DC:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And since you said that you yourself were in the town of Srebrenica -- And I will now stop. This is referring to the 11th of July. Let me start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And since you said that you yourself were in the town of Srebrenica, tell us, please, whether the town of Srebrenica was damaged; and generally, during your stay in the area, did you hear or see artillery weapons being fired?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some fire from artillery weapons, but very little. The fire was targeted at fortified Muslim positions. There was no need to do that. The town of Srebrenica was not shelled at all. Not a single shell fell on the urban part of the town. Not a single building was damaged when we entered the town on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have heard here that within a span of several hours, 200 shells were fired. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I said there was some artillery fire, but of a very limited extent, and it was mostly targeted at Muslim bunkers. Now, let me read the testimony of a witness who testified in this proceeding. His name was Zeljko Borovcanin. He testified in open session. And Mr. Borovcanin was asked, and I'm referring to the transcript starting at page 7020 and going over - I'm sorry - 7018 and going over to 7020. And in respect of shelling, what Mr. Borovcanin said, and I quote, on page 7018, lines 10 through 12, his answer to a question was:

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, until the 9th, my unit did not move from a starting position. Every day we heard occasional detonations, but these were occasional; they were not numerous. Now, Witness, I'm going to draw your attention back to some exhibits that we've previously discussed. If I could turn your attention, and with the assistance of the usher, if we could have 899 placed on the ELMO and the B/C/S version given to the General. What I'm going to do, General, is I'm going to read to you parts of the report from Mr. Borovcanin - I'm sorry - Mr. Becirovic's combat reports, and I'm going to ask you at the end to comment on the contents of the comment -- of the reports from Mr. Becirovic and the testimony that I've just read to you by two Defence witnesses. If I could direct your attention, first of all, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 899, under the section, the first section, dealing with the aggressor. I would like to read from a portion of this, about two-thirds of the way down: "Hundreds of shells were fallen on the lines of defence and civilian targets. As the day progresses, the aggressor's attacks seems to intensify, so that artillery shells are even now practically raining down on our defenders along all the lines of defence." It goes on to say in this report: "So far, over 20 shells were fallen on the town." Now, if we could turn to the next Exhibit, Mr. Usher, Prosecutor's Exhibit 900. This is a report again that was prepared by Mr. Becirovic on the 7th of July, and I'm quoting from the first paragraph, starting at the second sentence: "The aggressor has subjected the line of defence held by all units of the 28th Division of the Ground Forces to strong sniping and fire from anti-aircraft weapons throughout the day, and has frequently engaged in random tank-artillery fire against both the line of defence and civilian targets, practically covering the entire zone of Srebrenica with the shelling. In the course of the day, the very city centre of Srebrenica has frequently been the target of the aggressor's artillery fire, which is coming from a T-55 tank positioned above the town at Kula." General, if we could turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 901, which is Mr. Becirovic's report from Srebrenica on the 8th of July. And let me read you from the first paragraph of this, starting at the second sentence: "An enemy tank from the Kula is destroying the centre of Srebrenica on a daily basis, and at 1300 hours the enemy fired three guided missiles from that position on the town centre, causing enormous material damage." General, let's turn to the next exhibit, Exhibit 902, which is Mr. Becirovic's report dated the 9th of July. And I'll direct your attention to the first paragraph, starting to read from the second sentence: "The aggressor is conducting an infantry attack from the directions of Skelani and Podravanje, and the whole safe area came under fierce fire from artillery of all calibre. The town centre itself is being constantly shelled. Big concentration of aggressor's troops and armoured motorised forces have been observed today again. Four aggressor tanks are firing at the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road, and up to the time of this report, thousands of projectiles of various types have been fired." Let me turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 903, General, which is Mr. Becirovic's report from the 10th of July, starting again with the first paragraph, and I'm starting at the third sentence: "Infantry attacks are coming in waves and are being supported with four tanks operating from the direction of Ljubisavic, one tank from Pribicevac and all types and calibres of artillery pieces. At the same time, the whole zone of responsibility of the 28th Division of the KoV has come under attack, as well as civilian targets in the area." The last sentence of that first paragraph reads: "The centre of town is being continuously ravaged by artillery fire of the heaviest calibre." Now, General, I have a couple of questions. The first is: Is the information that is contained in Mr. Becirovic's report consistent with information that you or the army received about the shelling of the town of Srebrenica, the quantity of shells that were being fired into Srebrenica, and the intended targets, including civilians?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we don't have any documents of the 2nd Corps because the command of the 2nd Corps did report to the headquarters about all this. I have no doubt regarding the accuracy because -- of these statements because they were given by people who were there. And it is true that Srebrenica was attacked from those directions and that the town was shelled; that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what do you say about the two testimonies that I have read to you from Witness DC who was a member of the VRS, and Zeljko Borovcanin, both of whom say there was little shelling on the city of Srebrenica? Do you have any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. If the town of Srebrenica was demilitarised and if there were no military targets in it, the town should not have been shelled at all, not even slightly. It should not have been shelled at all. In town, there were civilians. I don't know what justification they had to target the city centre regardless of how many shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I have no additional questions. Thank you very much. No additional questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Perhaps we shall begin with the questions from the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or would you prefer a break, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will be using some exhibits, so we would use the break to prepare the documents with the registry's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Let's have a 20-minute break. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany the General out, please. So we are going to have our 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, General. You are now going to answer questions which Mr. Visnjic is going to put to you. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should like to ask the usher to give the witness Exhibit C2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, yesterday, you told Their Honours and the parties about a number of tables regarding statistics.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before we consider this exhibit, would you be kind enough to see the attached document on the basis of which I assume these tables were made. There is the organisational structure of the command, these three binders. My question has to do with the division command organisational structure. The department for intelligence affairs is directly subordinated to the commander. It is not part of the staff, am I right, of the headquarters staff?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me have a look at the table. It is Table 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you document C2 to prepare but my question does not relate to it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, would you please also help us find our way with the document so we can identify the document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received from the registry yesterday the attachments that the General used to explain the role and position of the 28th Division. So it is binder number one, if I can call it that, and the first document in it which is the organisational structure of the division command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. We have it now. It is a set of documents marked BR1, and then it is page two of that document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to facilitate things as the document is only in the Serbian language, in the left-hand corner, the third line from the top, you find the Department for Intelligence Affairs, that is the first box to the left, which, according to this table, is directly subordinated to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During the testimony of expert witnesses, both of the Defence and the Prosecution, we heard that the department for intelligence affairs mostly comes under the headquarters supreme command. I was wondering whether this same structure was accepted in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that is presented here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. So it differs from the structure that was established in the former JNA which you are also familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you now consider Exhibit C2, please. General Hadzihasanovic, could you tell Their Honours on the basis of which data did you prepare the total number of weaponry in Srebrenica and when that weaponry was reviewed? I'm mainly talking about the right-hand side of this table.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the situation in the 2nd Corps immediately prior to this, because there were periodic reports on effectives in the unit. Unfortunately, I didn't bring that document with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, let me now quote from an interview published in the newspaper Oslobodjenje on the 28th of August, 1996, and it is a conversation between Naser Oric, General Halilovic, and a third person, Rusmir Mahmutcehajic. Yesterday's witness confirmed the authenticity of this document, so I would like to draw your attention to a particular point made during that interview: "Naser was ordered to surrender the faulty and useless weapons, and that is how he acted. Three to four thousand rifles remained in our hands, not counting the Zepa Brigade. Let us round it off. About 3.500 men under arms, and we also had most of the heavy weaponry, and what was handed over to UNPROFOR was also accessible to them." General, does Naser Oric have any interest in mentioning a larger number of rifles in the hands of the 28th Division, or rather, the forces in Srebrenica, than they had?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this must be my answer, Mr. Visnjic: You should ask Naser that. I don't know. Secondly, I did not participate in those conversations, and what I have provided, I state with full responsibility that the data are correct. What someone may have said, I don't know on the basis of what they made such a statement. I'm really sorry. I didn't bring that document with me, so that you see that I didn't make it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you quite convinced that you had complete documentation regarding the state of weaponry of the 28th Division or the state in Srebrenica on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did, because I used a document which was for me an official document, which reached the 2nd Corps from the 28th Division. Whether somebody provided accurate data or not, I don't know, but I used that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to give the witness Defence Exhibit D52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we will remain with this pattern, with this table, until this exhibit reaches you. I should like to draw your attention to the column referring to the M57 hand-held launcher. Again I'm talking about the second half of the table and the situation regarding armaments in Srebrenica. Could you please look at the document of the command of the 28th Division of the 2nd of June, 1995. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know a person called Semsudin Salihovic, or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Semso? Do you know him or have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, was he a captain by rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't tell you for sure. I knew the ranks, names, and surnames of the commanders and chiefs of staff; however, I was not familiar with the other members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that he was responsible for logistics?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, since he signed such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: From this document, General, it can be seen that an oral order was given by the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division on the completion of combat sets, and within the framework of this order I wish to draw your attention to the mention of shells for the hand-held rocket launcher M57.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, if I say that on the 2nd of June, 1995, units of the 28th Division were given a total of 45 shells for the hand-held rocket launcher M57, on that day alone?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see 45, if I've added them up correctly. That is evident from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if 45 shells were distributed in just a single day, and if we assume that there wasn't a single such mine for the hand-held rocket launcher M57 there before the 2nd of June, doesn't this number already call in question the document that you don't have with you now? Because you said that the total number was 39; however, here we see that in a single day 45 were distributed.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I used the document of the command of the 2nd Corps - I'm sorry I didn't bring it - and that is the figure that I got from that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is six shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, General. The difference is six shells, on condition that the units didn't have a single mine on the 2nd of June, 1995. According to this, the difference is six shells.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, but without any condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to give the witness Defence Exhibit D47, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you told Their Honours yesterday that part of the materiel of the 28th Division were distributed by helicopter. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 7th of February, 1995. It is Exhibit D47. Is this a document which you yourself sent to the 8th Operative Group and the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of February, 1995? My signature is not on it. There were documents that I sent, but they're signed by me, so I don't know how this document was compiled. I did send documents, but each of my documents is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you send documents by electronic means to the command of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the document shown to you by the Prosecutor a moment ago, wasn't that also a document that was not signed by Mr. Becirovic and that was sent in a similar format?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I said that those were documents sent by Becirovic to the command of the 2nd Corps and not by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you, in the night between the 6th and 7th of February 1995, send to the territory of the enclaves a certain delivery of weapons, a certain consignment of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you a complete answer so as not to waste any time. I did dispatch a helicopter on the 31st of December, that was the first one. I dispatched a second one on the 10th of January; a third on the 6th of February; a fourth on the 11th of February; the fifth on the 16th of February; the sixth on the 22nd of February; the seventh on the 19th of April; the eighth on the 21st of April; the ninth on the 30th of April and the tenth on the 7th of May. And that is correct. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I had dispatched some helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this consignment, was there about 90.000 rounds, of which 66.150 were intended for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read out this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only rounds of 762 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent two kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Times 39?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica received 354,658 and Zepa, 173.600 rounds. This calibre, this times 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the consignment of the 18th of January, was there a total of 147.000 rounds?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of January? On the 18th of January, there were no deliveries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to give the witness a document dated the 18th of January 1995. I apologise, it's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what is a nitroglycerin rifle?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word speaks for itself. A rifle that has a drum with room for six or eight bullets, and the bullets contain nitroglycerin, as far as I am familiar with the technical properties, but the simplest way is to take the manufacturer's instructions and see in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of that rifle? Does it increase its lethal effect?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it -- that is a particular type of weapon. It isn't increased or decreased. That is how it is. Is it permitted by Geneva Conventions? I think it is. Other armies have it also.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you, in this document of the 18th of January 1995, intimate about 150.000 rounds for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're referring to a new document. The copy I have does not have an exhibit number for purposes of reference. I think it should be given one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had just noticed that. It's a new document, Mr. Visnjic, so perhaps it needs to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document is D179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is the number that I have given to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I should like to draw your attention to the third sentence from the bottom on this document. It says: "Please keep this confidential in relation to everyone, and especially in relation to UNPROFOR." What does this mean, General?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that at times certain matters were disclosed through UNPROFOR, and the secret that this was arriving was no secret. UNPROFOR saw the helicopters. They saw them in Tuzla as well. It was no secret for them or this document. The document is dated the 18th of January as an announcement, but because of weather conditions, we probably waited until the 6th of February when the helicopter was actually dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in one of the explanations you provided yesterday with regard to the needs that the 28th Division would have needed to break through the encirclement, you said that the 28th Division would have needed to have had 502 tonnes of cargo to carry with it; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I get that copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but it's your document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I should look for my own copy or could you give it to me. I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may consult your documents.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I take it out of my bag?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C5. This is a document which has not been marked for identification so could we mark it as C5, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Visnjic, because we already have a C5. If this is a new document ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it has already been marked, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was already marked C5.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the minimal needs of the 28th Division for its breakthrough from the encirclement, and the weight in tonnes as the total at the bottom, it says 502 tonnes of cargo which the 28th Division would have needed to carry with it during the breakthrough; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood. Allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 28th Division to have all the weaponry that it was lacking, according to these books, and in order to have five combat sets, which is a standard for offensive operations, we would have needed to transfer to them 502 tonnes of weaponry plus five combat ammunition sets. This is what we should have sent them to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can I go on from there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means that when a division embarks upon an offensive or a breakthrough, it needs all of that, but a soldier carries his weapon and one combat set. When a battalion is being transported, according to transport, in the transport vehicles, there should be another combat set -- I'm sorry, two combat sets. And in the brigade transport, another two -- I'm sorry, one, and in the division transport one, which makes it a total of five. As soon as a soldier has used his set, he gets it from the battalion, the battalion from the brigade, the brigade from the division, and the division asks a high-level command to provide it with extra ammunition to be able to continue the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly, hypothetically speaking, when the 28th Division embarked upon its breakthrough, it would have had to have logistics support which could have carried 502 tonnes of cargo to be able to use it up as they went along?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "to carry with it." I have just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My understanding is if the division is on the move, then at least the combat set belonging to the division must also move with the division?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This weight indicated includes the weight of side arms, personal weapons, ammunition, communications devices, and at least one canvas, one food rations, and at least five combat sets in the way I have described. To make a division capable of an offensive, it was our duty to provide it with this amount of cargo as there was no other way of delivering that cargo except by air. I made the calculations and gave you the figures as to what we should have done. Finally to wind up, I hope you understood my testimony yesterday when I said that the division, armed as it was and with the ammunition it had, was no obstacle or danger to anyone because it was, in combat terms, useless in view of the ammunition and weapons that were 50 per cent of the standard requirement; and every commander would be held responsible if he were to order such a unit to engage in combat without being properly equipped. That is the explanation that goes with these tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree -- I think we can agree that the 28th Division did not constitute any particular danger. However, if we take it in a context, together with the activity of the 2nd Corps, wouldn't it constitute a danger for any kind of division if they have a unit of 5.000 men behind them, armed men?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not armed, first of all. Then the second thing is that the status of the division was known. It was located in a protected area, and the town itself was a demilitarised town, and it did not have any weapons or equipment in it. So it did not constitute a danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 954 [as interpreted] of the transcript, you stated that the helicopter sorties were probably a signal for the Bosnian Serb army that something was brewing and that they might expect some combat operations to take place. However, you stated that with full responsibility, that that was not your objective. Did I understand correctly your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only perfectly normal that I stated that, and I have to tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us, first of all, if you said that or not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I would like to give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you a question, General. The 28th Division, that is, the Serb forces, were they ever officially informed by the BH army that the BH army was arming the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would they inform them of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the weapon delivery and helicopter sorties, were they coordinated with some other activities that the general staff of the BH army was conducting in relation to the overall objectives of the BH army concerning the enclaves and in the Podrinje area?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of objectives you are talking about. Helicopter sorties had nothing to do with that. Our objective was to try to alleviate the catastrophic situation in Srebrenica amongst the military and the population as well. We had to do something to calm them down and to provide our division with the minimal needs in case they are in a position to defend themselves. That cannot be prohibited by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have Exhibit D42 and 43, please, prepared for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what is the Grasshopper operation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to you what kind of communication devices we had and how we attempted to get them through to Srebrenica. Our first attempt was to do it on foot. We had a number of people who carried those communication devices to a certain location, and people from Srebrenica would come to that location to take it over, those communication devices, and that is why the operation was named Operation Grasshopper. So during that operation, we managed to send through some communication devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you have a look at the Exhibit D42, which is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do we have an English or a French version of the document? I would prefer a French one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, unfortunately, I prepared the documents in B/C/S for myself. I don't know whether my learned friend from the Prosecution has them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have an English version, and I will submit this to the usher to put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can help us with it, please, yes, so that we can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, is this a document which was issued by you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify something here. Sometimes, because of the selection of things that we could send through the usual communication devices, we would always put my name on the document, meaning that the document could be sent through the usual means of communication. Sometimes I personally would not sign the document, but the person who officially represented me at the time. I could give you a precise answer if I had the precise -- the exact document, and I can tell you if I myself signed it or not. In this period of time, in the month of December 1994, there were conflicts and attacks in the area of Zepa, so these instructions were issued so that a frontal conflict would not be accepted and so that direct conflicts would be avoided and an all-out fight be avoided in the area of Zepa. As regards the signature itself, if you had the original of the document, I could tell you exactly whether I signed it or not, whether I issued it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, Exhibit D43, could you place it in the same context as this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry to go back to the Exhibit D42 for a second. I should like to see the signature of General Hadzihasanovic on the document. Could we see it on the ELMO, please. The signature, that is, the place where we can see the final part of the document D42, the end of the document itself. I don't see it on the ELMO. I can't see it on the ELMO. Can you hear me? No, the English version, please. D42, the second page. Yes, that's the one. Thank you. General Hadzihasanovic, what does "Deputy Commander" and "Chief of Staff of Supreme Command" mean?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have both functions at the same time? Can you explain this to us? You were deputy commander and chief of SVK?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerned this particular period of time. When General Delic was present in the area, I didn't have that function. When he was absent from Bosnia and Herzegovina, until his return, I was fulfilling the function of the deputy commander. There is an organogram of the structure of the staff of Supreme Command, and that's what the situation was at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Hadzihasanovic, when the commander was present, were you Chief of Staff? That is, when he was absent -- and when he was absent, you were the deputy commander; was that the case?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I dealt with only certain urgent matters that could not wait. But everything that could wait for the commander would, of course, wait for his return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when the commander was present, you were an assistant, like other assistants, or was there any difference?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in charge of the staff itself. I was the Chief of Staff, that is, of a group of people, a group of military professionals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the staff had its own structure. If you have a look at the organogram, it would be clear to you what the position of the staff was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Visnjic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, let us stick with this document D42 for a while, but I should first like you to have a look at D43, because I have a few questions concerning that document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 62 written on my document. 43B?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the previous document, 42, which is still on the desk.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, could you tell the Judges what the strategic objectives of the BH army were concerning the area of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any strategic objectives, properly speaking. We had a directive issued every year which contained the description of what was to be achieved in that year and what kind of preconditions have to be met for those specific objectives to be implemented, those objectives which we usually defined in that instruction, directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will now read you something about what General Sead Delic said. He was the commander of the corps at the time of the fall of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Delic gave a statement to the Dani magazine on the 17th of March: "As a man from Podrinje, General Hadzihasanovic was in charge of organising things --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not been provided with a copy of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you know why you have to slow down. Would you please be more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. "As a man from the Podrinje area, General Hadzihasanovic was, on behalf of the General Staff, in charge of helping this area, so the overall coordination of the delivery of weapons and equipment was organised through him."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement made by General Delic. I did not have any specific obligation as a native from the Podrinje area - please let me finish - except for my personal duty that I felt I had. My duty was to provide organised helicopter sorties and the supply of equipment, because the corps did not have their own helicopters. They could not organise helicopter sorties, and it was my duty, my task, to coordinate that type of work. As to why he mentioned me as a native from the Podrinje area, I don't know. You should ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, did you issue an order for the sabotage incursions into the area around Srebrenica in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if I ordered such activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at D42B, which you still have in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. front of you, and read paragraph 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 3 of this order: "Organise sabotage activities in other parts by setting up ambushes along supply and evacuation routes of enemy forces primarily in the direction of Han Pijesak. Note: Do not carry out activities --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't see the end of the text.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you have misunderstood this document. If you want me to provide you with my explanation, I will be happy to do it. This document concerns a previous document which mentioned the Grasshopper operation. The name of the operation was changed into Ciko Kale. It concerns the dispatch of people from the direction of Tuzla, and also from Srebrenica to a specified locality, and also from Zepa to a locality which was specified in the document. The man who was in charge of leading the group from Tuzla was called Cikaric, and that's why we have the name of the operation Ciko. And the man from Srebrenica was nicknamed Kale, hence the name of the operation, which indicates how it all went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, after these two orders were issued, D42 and 43, which you have in front of you, did first helicopter sorties -- were first helicopter sorties organised on the 31st of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The movement along the ground and helicopter sorties were the only means of providing the area with the necessary equipment, because that's what these two operations were all about, Grasshopper and Ciko Kale. When we made our calculation as to how much equipment we needed, we decided, we found out, that it was not wise to send 10 to 30 or 40 people to carry out that job involving such heavy cargo. That's why we organised these first transports by helicopters, which carried medical supplies and the most urgent material, and it is correct that the first sortie was organised on the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, if it is correct that the Operation Grasshopper concerns what you have just told us, why, then, in D42, in paragraph 4, do you say the following: "We indicated how to treat UNPROFOR in letter, strictly confidential, 02-1/1597-1, but they must not be allowed to withdraw; and in case you cannot prevent them from doing so, take from them the weapons that we surrendered to them for safekeeping."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I haven't found the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: D42, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understand -- I mean I would understand this paragraph if I had the document that's mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, is it possible for UNPROFOR to have any reason whatsoever to withdraw from that situation concerning Srebrenica and Zepa in case you were transporting medical supplies, computers, and other equipment?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a specific mention of what helicopters were carrying in relevant documents. Second, as to UNPROFOR, reasons whether to pull out or not, I don't know whether they had to do it or not. Our goal was to have UNPROFOR remain in Srebrenica and observe for themselves what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, General, but we are talking about the document issued before the first helicopter sortie, the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 makes specific mention of a document whose contents I'm not familiar with. If you have the document, I'll be happy to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I will show you another document, D39. I will read for the record while you are looking at the document only the first part of the document. "To disarm UNPROFOR in the Vasionica camp, Srebrenica. The plan provides for seizing all materiel and technical equipment in UNPROFOR hands, infantry weapons, ammunition, communication equipment, clothing, footwear and other which can significantly benefit the BH army in the course of defending and liberating the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." General, this document was issued by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, 283rd Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which was sent to the command of the 8th Operative Group. Did you ever see this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you give us your comment on this document in light of what we have just discussed in relation to document D42, that is, the treatment of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read everything, just the first paragraph which I can comment, if we have enough time. But if you will allow me, I will read the whole document and give you my overall comment. I've read it. I don't know when, what, and how the people in Srebrenica were thinking, how their thoughts went. This is probably one of the ways in which their thinking went. If some things began to happen, how could they defend themselves? I don't know. I'm seeing this document for the first time, but that is my assumption. I said yesterday that I had information that at the end of 1994, in the Srebrenica enclave, that the situation was very bad with respect to humanitarian aid, the food for the people, and life in general there. It was very bad. And people wanted to leave regardless. We sought ways and means to calm the situation down there and one of the ways that the -- one thing that the army did was to bring the division in order to equip it, to arm it, so that the population could see this and have trust, put their faith in the army, that they were able to see that the army would be able to defend themselves.
