But this was probably the commander of the brigade thinking along those lines. I have no other comment but to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, an operative equivalent to the logistics forces, the forces in the rear with respect to the forces in the front, in other words, you as an experienced staff officer, how do you assess the ratio of forces when you infiltrate your forces into the enemy's rear? What effect would this have on the enemy's forces? Could you give us a rough idea, a ratio of forces?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how many men you engage, what you wish to aim at. You have to have a criteria, a standard. It all depends. You are asking me a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How many divisions into the rear of the enemy, how many men can they engage of the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That division was not infiltrated into the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm asking you a hypothetical question. General, as a staff officer, how many divisions would it require infiltrated into the rear of the enemy to engage enemy forces? Would the ratio be 1:1, 1:3, 1:5?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't do it that way, that is, just off the bat. You have to have a specific situation where the division is supposed to go, what the terrain is like, what the area is like, where the other forces are that can intervene, how much time they need, and so on and so forth. You have to know all this data of -- in a concrete situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, so far, you have been giving us generalised observations, how many combat ammunition sets or combat sets necessary and so on. That was an all-embracing, comprehensive, general assertion.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke of minimum quantities, the minimum quantity required. But if you want to analyse each specific situation, then you will have to do that and, according to that, to determine how much you need. To defend yourself for two or three days, you would have to have a minimum of one combat set. For a unit to go out at the level of a division, it must have five combat sets just to start out on an assignment. And how it can be supplied with materiel later on is another problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, that same staff school and the teachings of that school, does it say that the operative equivalent in the enemy rear is in the ratio of 1:3?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I mean the same type of doctrine that stipulates five combat sets.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do the same military principles apply on the basis of which you have claimed that a division needs five combat sets in order to break through an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say five.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said a minimum of five.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a division to be assigned this task, it must have that number of combat sets. Now, as to the particular assignment, we would have to calculate what is necessary for an assignment, additional materiel for the assignment to be carried out. For example, if the division doesn't do anything in peace time, it would have to have that kind of -- those kinds of sets as a standard, basic set.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, operative standards of the forces in the enemy's rear, to get back to my question. How many enemy forces can your unit engage?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are alluding to the 28th Division --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I am not alluding to anything. I'm asking you a hypothetical and theoretical question.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given an answer to your hypothetical and theoretical question, and I have said that you have to have basic data where the unit is being sent to, what depth, what area, what its assignment is, what the encirclement is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But General, is there a minimum? You mentioned five combat sets without which an order of this kind cannot be given. So I am asking you for a minimum now. Give us a minimum.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The existence of a unit and the -- its equipment is a standard. Now, if you want to infiltrate them into the enemy rear, this is a combat operation for which statistics, mathematical assessment will have to be made. So there is no particular standard. You can't quote a standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, breaking through an encirclement, is that a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that the equivalent of the forces in the rear as to engage in the enemy forces is in the ratio of 1:3?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you there because, for me, that is a generalised specification. I would have to know the actual concrete situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you compile a plan and even draw a relief for the liberation of Podrinje as is claimed in the article of the 17th of March 2000, as General Sead Delic said in the article published on the 17th of March 2000?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Sead Delic said. There was a relief specifying the front lines throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only in Srebrenica. It was a visual image, and people who were authorised to do the planning or the decision makers were able to see the situation as it was in the field. And amongst others, on this relief, they had Srebrenica as well, but it was overall relief for Bosnia-Herzegovina. It had Sarajevo and other parts as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the 2nd Corps of the BH army, did it issue at the beginning of the summer, end of June, beginning of June, that is, an order to the 28th Division to organise sabotage incursions into Serbian territory around the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You said the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you, yourself, issue an order to the 28th Division for incursion into Serb territory in the environs of the enclave and for carrying out sabotage action?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue to the 28th Division, except that I should bring it up to combat readiness. I issued no other orders apart from that order to the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you, at any time, issue orders to the 28th Division bypassing the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, the 2nd Corps. Did you issue orders to the 28th Division avoiding or sidestepping the command of -- the chain of command of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to helicopter flights and equipping the divisions, I did send down orders of this kind, but the command of the 2nd Corps, from the very beginning, knew of that undertaking and I explained why, because the 2nd Corps did not have authority over the helicopters. I had to communicate directly and to send what was in the helicopters because the 2nd Corps didn't know what was in the helicopters. And in a previous agreement, the 2nd Corps knew what was going to happen when transport of this kind was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to read a part of a statement made by Sead Delic in answer to a question that was asked him. The journalist asks, "The Chief of Staff, General Hadzihasanovic, issued an order for sabotage incursions into Serb-held territory in the environs of Srebrenica without reinforcing the defence lines on the basis of which data and information was that order issued? That is my question for you." No, I'm reading. And General Delic answers, "As far as I know, it was an order which the 2nd Corps received, but it was not linked unless it reached them in the line towards Zepa and Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No orders went out from the headquarters like that. You are reading from a newspaper article. If I had a document, I would be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I will continue the quotation. "In that aim, an order arrived which specified that, wherever possible, sabotage and other operations were to be undertaken in order to engage the enemy, in order to inflict casualties to the enemy, and to stop him from introducing units into the area. I don't know whether an order of this kind went to Srebrenica and Zepa, but it was a period when we intensified our sabotage incursions and smaller attacks on individual features which means that the order did exist."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is within the context of a conversation between a journalist and the gentleman in question. I would be able to give a comment if this were founded on a document, then I would be able to say yes, that it is so or it is not so, and it is a comment of those two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, General Krstic has asked for a break, if possible, and I have 15 more minutes of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the reasons you have specified, we are going to take a break. Perhaps we shall take a lunch break at this point. Let us take advantage of this opportunity and have a lunch break and then see how we stand, how much more we need for today. I shall first ask the usher to accompany General Hadzihasanovic out of the courtroom before we adjourn for lunch. We are now going to adjourn for a 50-minute lunch break. --- Break taken at 12.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May I ask the usher to give the witness Exhibit D36 and to prepare for the witness also Defence Exhibit D67, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, while you're reviewing that document, allow me to remind you that yesterday you spoke about your efforts to reorganise the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and particularly the units in the area of the enclaves. General, this document, issued by the command of the 8th Operative Group, does it in content correspond to the situation in which the BH army found itself regarding the reorganisation of its units at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am able to understand this document, Mr. Attorney, there are several questions here addressed by the command of Operative Group 8 regarding the reorganisation; for instance, how to register people who are not from the area, who are from other municipalities and do not know their speciality from the former JNA, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, there's no need to go into details. Let me ask you whether this content corresponds, more or less, to what you were endeavouring to achieve through your bodies, with the aim of improving the organisation of the 8th Operative Group, and does this document reflect the problems that the 8th Operative Group at the time was encountering?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our order existed regarding the reorganisation of the army, and one of those orders was probably addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps. What kind of explanations the corps gave to the Operative Group, I don't know. Clearly, from this document, the Operative Group is asking for explanations of certain points, and there's nothing doubtful about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But the time frame corresponds. General, let me ask you about the last sentence of this document on page 2. In the English version, it is all on one page. The last sentence reads: "Could you therefore, because of the combat activities planned to link up the 8th Operative Group and the 2nd Corps, complete the implementation of this order by the end of the planned activities and inform us of this a little before." General, my question is: What are those planned combat activities to link up the 8th Operative Group and the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were probably some thoughts given to it, but I'm not aware of any plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me read to you once again a part of a statement made by General Sead Delic in his interview of the 17th of March, 2000, relating to plans for the liberation of Podrinje, that Sead Delic in his previous statement claims that you were the author of those plans. And then he goes on to say: "One plan was the deblocking of Sarajevo, the second of Podrinje. Because of the political situation at the time, the preference was given to the deblocking of Sarajevo. Also, from the General Staff, plans of activities were requested which would be undertaken in the case of offensive activities against Podrinje. As for offensive operations linked to the deblocking of Sarajevo, it was our conclusion that the safe areas, in accordance with international law, enjoy a special status. No combat operations, no attacks, even though, from the military point of view, they were the most sensitive places in our overall deployments, that is, the enclaves." General, would you agree with that statement made by General Sead Delic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you keep asking me about what somebody else said. His thoughts and his positions I can neither share or criticise or comment on them. All I can say is that that was his personal affair, what he said. As for the General Staff and plans related to Srebrenica and deblocking it, no such plan existed. There is no dilemma over that, but we kept sinking over what should be done with the enclaves if something should happen to them. There were such reflections, assessments, thoughts, what to be done, and one of those conclusions was to set up this unit to appease the situation at the end of 1994, and I do know of that objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The execution of sabotage activities behind the lines of the Serb forces was one -- was it a part of the plans to liberate Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the General Staff, there were no such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit D67, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, while you are reviewing this document, for the record, I will read a part of it, paragraph 1 and a part of paragraph 2 of this document. "The soldiers of the 28th Division of the ground forces located in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, although burdened with serious problems with food and the obligation to preserve in their zone of responsibility the free territories that they hold, decided to make as large a contribution as possible to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina's struggle against the aggressor, and to that end, strengthened their activity in the depth of the aggressor's temporarily occupied territory. While carrying out reconnaissance, sabotage groups of the 28th Division of the ground forces encountered aggressor reconnaissance sabotage groups several times and opened fire. In this reconnaissance period, the following results were achieved..." And then those results are enumerated. Let me also read the first sentence from the second paragraph, which says: "In order to prevent enemy forces from sending additional troops from the areas around Srebrenica and Zepa to the Sarajevo front, two sabotage actions were carried out in the vicinity of Srebrenica, one on the 23rd of June 1995 in Osmace, and another on the 23rd of June 1995 in Bijelo Stijenje near Koprivna with the following results being achieved..." In continuation of this document, General, there is a description of further activities by the reconnaissance and sabotage groups of the 28th Division of the ground forces and, as reflected by this document, it is stated that, "According to our estimates, more than 40 Chetniks have been liquidated though we have unconfirmed reports that the aggressor's losses amount to 71 soldiers." General, this report was addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this report for the first time. If it was sent, then somebody should be held responsible for its accuracy. I see this report for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 28th Division, General, according to this report, at least in two places, makes mention in paragraphs 2 and 3 and then also in paragraph 4, mentions the reason for these operations, and that is to prevent additional forces being sent to the Sarajevo front or, rather, engaging the forces of Republika Srpska within the enclaves. General, what is stated in this document, does that fit into the plan for the deblocking of Sarajevo which the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what was the control implemented by high level commands of Bosnia-Herzegovina over their forces?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The control was effected in the force of orders, suggestions, instructions, but we couldn't have physical control over them, a team of the General Staff or the command of the 2nd Corps to go physically to Srebrenica and check the situation there. That was not possible. Everything went through papers, documents. And what was ordered undertaken, we did not have the chance to physically check.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, but you did regularly receive reports from the 28th Division, 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you control the work of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the 28th Division is a rather large unit. Is it possible for their commanders to undertake certain actions arbitrarily?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they did or not, I don't know. They shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, is it possible that this document reflects an order received by the 28th Division to strengthen activities, intensify activities, in order to assist the BH army in deblocking Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the deblocking of Sarajevo, we did send an order to other fronts to intensify activities, and to other corps, which is only normal to facilitate this part of our task. But I know exactly that in that order regarding Srebrenica and Zepa, nothing specific was stated. Whether the command of the 2nd Corps sent anything like that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the command of the 2nd Corps, did they inform you that they had sent anything to Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know where the command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica was stationed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to communications, near Igrisnik, south-west, as far as I know. And it probably changed its locations because of the conditions. The command of the 2nd Corps must know that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And where was the command of the Protective Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which protective battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let us move on to another topic. General, I will read to you again a passage from a statement by General Delic, so I'll read a part of the statement -- no, I won't be reading from General Delic, but part of a statement of Naser Oric, in an interview on the 28th of August, 1996, regarding the humanitarian situation in the enclave: [As read] "Smuggling, there was some. Do you know or not? There were six or seven thousand inhabitants of Zepa, and they reported three times as many, and that is how they had food. Then they would sell the surplus. From the Dutch, you couldn't buy anything, not a gramme of salt. But the Ukrainians were such that they would sell everything. They would only keep their slippers if necessary." General, and another portion of another statement, again by General Sead Delic in his interview of the 17th of March, when he says, I quote: "There are some statements and indicators that humanitarian aid was distributed exclusively under the wing of the military and not through civilian authorities, and that it was distributed in the way individuals thought fit." General, the report sent from the enclaves, did they exaggerate the humanitarian problems for the reasons given here by Mr. Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why you are asking me questions about other people's statements. To give you an exact reply as to whether they were exaggerated or not, one would have to check it out physically, which was not possible. I just know that from the command of the 2nd Corps, we received reports that the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica was disastrous. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, as a Superior Command, did you know that humanitarian aid in the Srebrenica enclave was being distributed exclusively under the authority of the military?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did anyone, ever, through intelligence or some other reports, inform you about this? You were the Chief of Staff, and I assume that the entire intelligence reports reached you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your assumption, but it is not true. Only the intelligence reports that were necessary for taking stock of the military situation on the ground, the movement of units by the aggressor, the situation, where which unit was, what their intentions were. But I didn't engage in these other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are not familiar with the humanitarian situation in detail?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, but I knew that in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves the humanitarian situation was bad. As for the details, I was not familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So General, you did receive certain reports about the humanitarian situation in your staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, "humanitarian situation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript. You did, after all, receive some reports on the humanitarian situation, and not only on the military situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you consider information that the people in the enclave and the military are hungry, that people haven't got enough to eat, as humanitarian reports, then I did receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And that is all you received about the situation there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in a report shown to you by the Prosecution, it is stated that the humanitarian situation is such that the population has nothing to eat and that the army, in a day or two, would run out of supplies, if I am paraphrasing correctly. Does that mean that the army, in terms of food supplies, was better supplied than the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us go on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, excuse me for interrupting you. Before the break, you told us that you needed a quarter of an hour. You've already used twice as much. Do you need a third quarter of an hour or are you going to finish soon, so that we have some idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I need another five to seven minutes, on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown OTP Exhibit 614, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And General, when did the Main Staff of the BH army learn of the start-off of the column from Susnjari towards free territory, or, better still, according to your information, on the 12th, or rather, the 11th, at midnight, or a few minutes after midnight, that is, on the 12th, early in the morning, did the Chief of Staff report that he was heading out towards Udrc Baljkovica, and that at 0220 hours the command of the 2nd Corps had forwarded urgently this information to the Main Staff of the BH army? I'm talking about the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the staff and the commander cautioned and were not in favour of the 28th Division abandoning the safe area, and they did not have an order or permission from the headquarters to go anywhere. On the 11th, in the evening, in the village of Susnjari, the division command, and I think some people from the political authorities, made that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is not disputed that a decision was taken. What I'm interested in is --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they started out, we lost contact with them, and we didn't communicate with them until the 15th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff of the BH army at 0220 hours receive an urgent telegram or cable or in some other way a report from the command of the 2nd Corps, informing them that they were moving along the Udrc-Baljkovica road?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Because, as I say, the last contact that we had was that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the determination of the axis Udrc-Baljkovica, was that the axis of withdrawal towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "axis"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Udrc-Baljkovica route, is that, in fact, the route along which the units withdrew?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I can show you from my notebook the exact sequence of the villages towards Crni Vrh, crossing the asphalt road from Kalesija to Zvornik, that is that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And that is where you met the units?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the very exit in the early morning. I had already arrived because I wasn't at headquarters at the time. I was somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did the Main Staff of the BH army and the 2nd Corps, did they already on the 12th at 0220 hours know the route upon which the column was withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 12th at 0220?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. On the 12th, the first reports reached us, I can't remember the details now, were brought by the women and children who arrived in the area of Kladanj. So the first information as to where they might go and what was happening in Srebrenica reached us like that. Officially, from the 28th Division, we received nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 11th at midnight, the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, did he report to the staff for the last time, and after that the communication was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in contact with us on the 11th in the evening, and after that, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff, was it informed urgently from the command of the 28th Division at 0220 in the morning about it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably, but I don't know exactly because I was not there at the time; I was close to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can we see the Exhibit 614. General, let me draw your attention to paragraph 3 of this document and I will have only one question in respect of that. General, as the Chief of Staff of the BH army, did you know that the VRS had established a corridor, had opened a corridor for the passage of the members of the 28th Division through their lines and positions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not open a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you know at the time that Colonel Vinko -- Lieutenant Colonel at the time, actually, Vinko Pandurevic, was negotiating with Semso Muminovic, one of the officers, concerning that issue?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the breakthrough in the Poljanje region, yes, there was communication between him and Pandurevic. Actually I don't know that man, but he did communicate with someone, and he said that, "You should let the men get out of the area. You have done enough harm." As to what "getting out" meant, the front line was pierced at one particular point, but the people were still coming in from the rear. So he was asking him to let the others go through the lines and leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did that actually happen in the way it is described here?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know was that the Zvornik Brigade was in Srebrenica but that certain elements of the Zvornik Brigade were also there, and according to the people who were there, the Zvornik Brigade, in that area, did not have many troops and that the passage simply went through. The people went through the lines. It was not a show of goodwill of their commanders because they simply didn't have enough troops for that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I now realise that you actually knew where the Zvornik Brigade was, but at that point in time, you didn't know where your units were; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "your units."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the units of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we are talking about the units of the 28th Division, I said that we were not in contact with them at the time, and we did not have precise information as to their whereabouts. The forward command of the 2nd Corps heard them on the 15th of July in the evening through Motorola, and they established contact with them on the 16th of July when they reached Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, would it refresh your memory if I told you that the Zvornik Brigade returned as early as the 15th of July in its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. You're referring to the Zvornik Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if you didn't know the whereabouts of the elements of the 28th Division but you knew about the direction they had taken, could you not assume, theoretically speaking, as to the point -- as to the location they would finally emerge and reach the lines held by the BH army and were any offensive activities undertaken with the purpose of joining, reuniting with the units of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned about it only on the 16th of July, in the morning hours of the 16th of July, not on the 15th of July. If we had done anything prior to that point in time, we would have, perhaps, made a mistake. We would have attempted to do something on a different location and they would have come through at another spot along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. General Hadzihasanovic, we will have a few questions for you from the bench. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can shed some light on a few of your assertions whether in your testimony or in the -- what you called I think here the information you gave, written on the 24th of January. First, concerning the column you mentioned which was formed on the 11th of July. Apparently, you said it was leaving to the free territory and it contained the 28th Division command and municipal authorities. How many civilians were there, and why did the civilians join it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, just a second. I would like to find that piece of information. It is true that the command of the division was there together with some commanding officers, members of the staff, in the village of Susnjari where the command of the division was located. And in the course of the 11th of July, in that area, members of the division assembled together with, according to the information I have from what I could learn from the statement of the members of the staff and others, around 6.000 to 7.000 civilians in the area of Susnjari. That is, the military and the civilians were together. The civilians in question were people who were men of military age, able-bodied men, and they did not trust in the impartiality of anyone in terms of surrender. Only women, children, and elderly went to the UNPROFOR base. There was justified suspicion that every civilian, able-bodied man, could be harmed simply of the fact that he was of the military age, and that is why the reason why they all assembled there. They wanted to follow the military wherever they would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said it was a justified fear. Why was it justified?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fear was justified because in the course of previous years, in 1992 and 1993 in particular, because of the events that took place in that area and, in particular, in the municipalities of the Zvornik, Bratunac, and Vlasenica, and also after the fall of the Cerska, Kamenica, and Konjevic Polje enclaves, people knew, in view of those events, what could happen to them and they were simply afraid that such things might happen again. As they were fleeing the area Cerska - Konjevic Polje - Bratunac, those people finally ended up in the Srebrenica enclave, so they had justified fears as to what might happen to them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you said there were 7.000 civilians, so how much would be their percentage in the column?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said when they were -- you just mentioned the people who managed to come out from the column were manhunted easily in the way from Srebrenica to Vlasenica. What did you mean by "manhunt?" Fighting, fighting with the soldiers, the Muslim -- Serb soldiers, or chased just indiscriminately?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part of the column, which was initially between 12 and 15 kilometres long, when that second part of the column was shelled, the civilians which were mainly members of that portion of the column were hit. Regardless of the fact that those people were not armed, they were targeted and they were subsequently captured; at least, that is what the people who managed to get out told us. They described it as manhunt, the people I had an opportunity to talk to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And it was indiscriminate, indiscriminate, according to what was, in your opinion, established or told to you, old and young and resisting or non-resisting?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke about the -- you said, exactly, that the 28th Division was useless in combat terms and not capable to engage in combat, and hence did not constitute any danger to the other party. And you also spoke with the Defence counsel of the helicopters which were sent, I think it was from December 31st to mid-May. In spite of these helicopters, the 28th Division was completely out of combat and useless, or did these helicopters give it some, let us say, power to fight?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was transported in helicopters was in such a small percentage for the division to be made useful. All the data that I have supplied you with in the documents that I have brought with myself is contained in that number, and the percentages that are given in these documents indicate the strength of the division. It is all included in the figures that you have in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in your opinion, it was out of -- the division was completely useless for combat, adequately?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The division was not useful in combat terms. Its capability, generally speaking, was not more than 30 to 40 per cent. As I say, generally speaking, if we take into account all kinds of weapons and ammunition, in some departments they were armed 50 per cent of the full capacity; and in certain other departments, zero. So it was useless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned your report and so on. In fact, I detected that you were speaking about the quantity of weapons, rifles, and you also said that -- you gave the number, as you said, and you said they represented no threat to the Serbian forces. Did the Serbian forces know that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have known that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, would they be expecting an enemy of calibre, who could be of great resistance, or were there indications that there were no weapons? Was there some kind of checking? Did UNPROFOR check the demilitarisation? Was there any understanding about that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was to -- was supposed to supervise the weapons that had been handed over to them, and they were supposed to observe the movements of troops on the boundaries of the safe area, so I know -- I think that the UNPROFOR must have known about the quantities of weapons of various units deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they would communicate that to the other party?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything to that effect, but it is my assumption that it was possible for them to convey such conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you receive any - not you, but I mean the 28th Division - receive any protests from the UNPROFOR that did not respect the demilitarisation and that they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as the issue of demilitarisation is concerned, the way I understand the relevant document, it referred to the urban area of the Srebrenica town, whereas the term "safe area" concerns a wider territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And concerning the urban area of Srebrenica, it received shelling?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It did. And was the shelling also indiscriminate, or in a way they wanted to have a target, military targets?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no military targets in the town itself. As far as I know, at the time the agreement on demilitarisation was signed, one of the reasons -- one of the ways of avoiding the shelling of the town was to sign that there were no military targets in the town. A soldier could not -- was not allowed to walk around the town with a rifle; however, a soldier could go to the town and visit his family without his weapon, if he had any family living in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In your information or submission of 24th of January, you mentioned that 172.000 non-Serbs in the zone were ethnically cleansed. Can you just have some more specification what you mean by "ethnically cleansed"? What did it cover?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the establishment of the Srebrenica enclave in the area of the Zvornik and Bratunac and Visegrad, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak municipalities, as well as the municipality of Rogatica, Sokolac, and Pale, which was, according to our estimates, the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, from those areas, ethnically -- there was no population there. The area was ethnically cleansed, either through detention or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. persecution. And when the -- I think that about 150.000 non-Serbs lived there before that. The number increased after the fall of Srebrenica, of course, but it only concerned the territory of the Srebrenica municipality. So as regards the territory of the municipalities that I have indicated, 170.000 non-Serbs were missing from that area in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And after that, did they find out how much remained in the area, or come back, or that's too -- or killed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that those people are no longer there in that area. Some were killed, some were detained in camps, some were evicted from the area. They are simply no longer there. Some of them eventually found themselves in the area of Tuzla, Kladanj, Sarajevo, Central Bosnia, some ended up in third countries, the final result being that they were no longer in that area. It was only after the signing of the Dayton Accords and sometime later that those people started coming back to the area. At the time of the Srebrenica events, that number of people was no longer in the area that I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And perhaps a last question concerning the report of Major Becirovic on the humanitarian situation, when he said, on the 6th -- I think it was the 6th of July, 7th of July: "More civilians have been registered as having died from hunger and asking for quantities of food." What was done about that? Were you able to send him food or was the food prevented from reaching?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passage of food was interrupted, because the last convoy carrying the food did not reach its destination, the UNHCR convoy. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the VRS army didn't allow it to go through. In those days, they even prevented the relief of UN units who were stationed in Srebrenica, and immediately prior to the fall of Srebrenica, as far as I know, soldiers from the UN observation posts were being captured. Access to Srebrenica was not allowed, simply speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we're trying to finish with this witness. Would General Krstic like a break? Could you speak to him, please, or can we continue? Could you speak to the General, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General, you've given us a very detailed account of the deficiencies in equipment and manpower of the 28th Division on the eve of the fall in Srebrenica. I wonder if you can give us, very briefly, bottom line, as it were, a comparative analysis of what your impression was of the strength of the Serb forces in the area. In other words, if the 28th Division was only 50 per cent up to par on equipment or -- and I think you said 30 or 40 per cent in other categories, would you say that the Drina Corps forces in the area of the enclave were twice as well equipped, twice as -- just a rough estimate of the comparative adequacy.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can go broader than that but I shall be very brief. They were not only twofold, they were more than that as far as ammunition is concerned. As for rifles and other equipment, they had sufficient quantities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I believe you said that once the column got moving and had reported to the superior commands of the 2nd Corps, that they were on their way to Tuzla, the superior commands lost communication with the column and had no further communication until later on with the forefront of the column which was getting ready to break through. You also said, though, that the first inkling that the superior commands in the army had as to what had happened at Srebrenica or Potocari came when the women and children reached the free territory from the buses. I was wondering how would you find out from the women and children who were evacuated on the buses from Potocari what had happened to the column? I mean, because they didn't actually have any contact with the column. How much were you able to find out from the women and children, and when did you find out about the fact that the column had been cut off and what, if anything, had happened to them vis-à-vis the manhunt that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first refugees that reached the region of Kladanj that were transported there, between Kladanj and Vlasenica about midway, there is a tunnel. Prior to that tunnel, they got off, and they arrived on foot. And in Kladanj, we also had a brigade that was on the front line. When the people appeared, people were running up to them to help them. Among others, officers from that brigade collected the first information from them, and the civilians were then transferred to Tuzla where a tent settlement was being prepared for them to -- where they could rest, and eat, and so on. So that was the first information that we got from -- on what was happening in Potocari and that the army was on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did those women and children or the people who got off the buses, did they tell you or did they tell the people there about the separation of the men and their fears or ignorance of what had happened to the men in Potocari? Not the men in the column, but the men that had been separated in Potocari? Is that the first time that superiors in the army learned about the fact that the men were not arriving on buses any time near the women; they had been deflected off someplace else?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You gave us some figures or estimates of a range between 8.300 and 9.700 people who were killed or -- this is my question, or missing, 2.600 of whom were from the 28th Division. I was wondering whether or not those estimates of people killed are estimates of people missing, we simply don't know what happened to them. Or if they are of estimates of people killed, are they divided between people killed in combat and people killed by the executions? In other words, are those figures broken down?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that 2.628 soldiers of the division that we can say with relative accuracy, that that is the number. Why we say that is that we had a list of members of the division, and then we checked those who were there, and those who were missing. Their destiny, those of the missing ones, probably differed. Some may have been hit by a shell, some having surrendered his weapons, rounded up, in various ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, when you heard later on, and I understand this was, as it were, after the fact, when you found out what had happened in terms of the people who were captured in the second part of the column, who were captured, some of whom were detained, as we know, many of whom, a large portion of whom were subsequently killed, did you receive information at that point as to who it was that was taking custody of these people? I mean who it was that was capturing them and who it was that was taking them off to the areas of detention, and even who it was that was subsequently executing them? Were your informants as to what had happened to them able to inform you of any of those facts and, if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer in general terms that it was the army of Republika Srpska and members of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Both, is that right? This has been talked about a great deal in the trial, that's why I asked you the question. But your information is that both members of the MUP and members of the VRS were engaged in the capture of these people.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at what point did the army, the 2nd Corps or your headquarters, first obtain information that people had been executed; not just captured, taken away, but actually executed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that the first information was received both by civilians and the army when those first women left Kladanj and arrived in Tuzla, because there were executions in the immediate vicinity of the UN Compound in Potocari. And the separation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There weren't mass executions in the immediate area of the Potocari. There may have been random killings, but the mass executions, as I understand from all the evidence we've received, were started around the 13th, but they were some distance away. So that was my basic question: How do the women and children know about the executions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because as the vehicles passed through certain areas, they saw them by the road, saw dead men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Did they -- did these informants have information to relay about who was involved in carrying out the executions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they, too, claimed that it was done by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I just have three more questions. In the information which you were able, at the time, but maybe primarily later to find out from the people, the army people who actually made it across, the civilians who made it across, and some of the survivors later on who made it across, were you or the superior officers able to gain any impression of who was, in effect, running the show as far as the capturing and the executions? Which particular Generals of the VRS seemed to be in charge, seemed to be giving the orders, seemed to be running the operation? The operation I'm now talking about being the capture, detention, and subsequent execution?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the command of the Drina Corps was present in the area of Srebrenica, but we also knew that General Mladic was there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Were you able to get any impression from your informants as to who was, again, kind of in charge of the operation, the manhunt, the killings part of the operation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the command staff of this command was there and General Mladic, I assume it was them, because we couldn't hear it or feel it. The distance between the column and those who were shooting was quite considerable. You couldn't see or hear it. But since they were there, they were probably informed about it. I have no hard evidence about that, but they were their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is one directed to your knowledge of the -- all of the operations that were going around in that area, not then, but previously that you've referred to before. I'm interested in your views as to what factors you think -- I realise you don't know, none of us know, but what factors you think would have led the VRS, the MUP, whoever did it in this instance, to execute these thousands of Muslim men following the fall of Srebrenica as opposed to taking them, putting them in camps, putting them as prisoner exchanges, the kinds of things that were more typical of the other operations that we've seen. What do you think led to this vast scope of immediate executions in such a short period of time, just dealing with the fall and the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day, I cannot explain or answer that question myself to myself. What occurred to those people in the army of Republika Srpska, in MUP, to simply go and kill those people who were innocent, believe me, I have not given myself an answer to that question yet as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. And this is my very last one, it's a hypothetical, but let me ask you, based on your military experience: If, and it is a hypothetical, if a commander whose area of responsibility encompasses a particular geographical area, if that commander should learn - this is a hypothetical - if that commander should learn that, in fact, his own superior, his own superior was using some of the forces under his command to commit war crimes in that area, if he learned that, what do you think his responsibility militarily would be?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he would have to demand an explanation for it. Secondly, if he disagreed with those procedures, he would have to give up his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. General Hadzihasanovic, I, too, have a few questions for you. Perhaps they are small ones as I am the last. There is one thing that I would particularly like to understand properly. As far as I have been able to understand, the 28th Division was created more or less the 15th of March 1995, then came the 8th Operational Group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in the structure of the 2nd Corps, there was the 8th Operative Group which, due to the reorganisation, was restructured in personnel and equipment on the 15th of March 1995. And from then on, it was called the 28th Division officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Why was this division created for a particular area which was or should have been demilitarised? You gave us some reasons such as quite appeasing the population of Srebrenica, but are there any other reasons for creating at such a late date especially for a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We completed the first reorganisation for Sarajevo in 1992. In Tuzla, it wasn't done in 1992, it was done in 1993 and during 1993. It depended on the area. Because of the inability to communicate with Srebrenica, this dragged on until such a late date, but the main reason was that there was no means by which we could send them the documents on the basis of which they would reorganise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. Another aspect that I should like to mention: A witness in this courtroom said that 18 officers based in Srebrenica left for training in Zenica. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us what was the justification for this departure, and specifically whether their departure had anything to do with the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, allow me to explain. We had a wartime officer school in Zenica; that was its precise name. And from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from all other units, even from Gorazde, we had people undergoing training there. On one occasion, there was a complaint from Srebrenica through the command of the 2nd Corps as to how come no one could undergo training from Srebrenica. It's as if they had been written off, that is how they put it, as if nobody was taking care of them at all. Probably their turn would have come anyway, but we speeded up the process because of this suggestion, if I may call it that, on the part of the command and their feeling of being neglected. So this number of men were transferred to Zenica to graduate from the school and then turned back. So they have -- it has nothing to do with the combat operations there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 18 officers, did they go back to Srebrenica or did they stay outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were returned to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, General: Was there any parallel between the operations in Tuzla and the column? That is, when the Bosnian authorities learned of the difficulties of the column, did they organise a coordinated operation to help the people to leave? Was there any movement of that kind and in that direction?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps had prepared units to assist the breakthrough. The only problem was where they would emerge, what particular part of the front line so that we wouldn't make a mistake. And on the 16th in the morning, it was known exactly where they might emerge, and that is where they were assisted. The 212th Brigade of the 2nd Corps made a break through the front lines there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did people choose Tuzla and not Zepa, for instance? Do you have any indication of that? I mean the column.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they estimated that even if they went to Zepa sometime in the future, they would suffer the same fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one might say that their choice was linked to the reasons that led them to leave.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question which we have already touched upon to a certain extent is: After the fall of Srebrenica, were there any contacts with the Serb forces, and specifically, with General Mladic? We know already that during the movement of the column there were some negotiations, specifically with Vinko Pandurevic. I'm saying after all these things, were there any contacts, military contacts, between the Serbs and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: In your opinion, or rather, as far as you know -- no. Let me rephrase that. Do you know when General Krstic took over command of the Drina Corps? Do you have any information on the part of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally must say that I do know General Krstic. We graduated from the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade. We are of the same generation. That he became commander, I heard for the first time in a statement made by Mr. Karadzic on television, when he said he was -- he was commenting, making comments about General Mladic, and then he said, "We have some other highly qualified commanders as well. For instance, General Krstic is now in the Srebrenica operation. I approved his plan. He is a capable Corps Commander," words to that effect. I'm paraphrasing. And since that statement was broadcast on the television of Republika Srpska, reception of TV programmes in Sarajevo was possible. Until then, we had information that General Krstic was the Chief of Staff in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any idea when that was, the date of the statement made by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have been just before Srebrenica or during Srebrenica, during the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a document or anything else on the basis of which I could say with precision when that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you are saying that this statement was made, in your view, by President Karadzic just before or even in the course of the events of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately afterwards, very close to the fall of Srebrenica. It must have been around about then. Maybe five or ten days after that. I really can't remember. But I do remember him saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To try to be slightly more precise, can you pinpoint in time? When you say "the fall of Srebrenica," what date do you have in mind? What particular date?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our records, it is the 11th, the 11th, when the army of Republika Srpska entered the town of Srebrenica. It has been recorded as that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how many days before or after the 11th of July are you talking about that you heard the statement by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about his statement, but I don't know the exact date when he made that statement. I really can't remember it. I didn't take note of it anywhere, so I wouldn't like to say something that is not accurate. But he did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But in his words, if you know, did President Karadzic say that he was going to appoint him or that he had already been appointed; that he was going to appoint General Krstic as Corps Commander or whether he was saying that he had already been appointed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this is what he said, and I'm paraphrasing. General Mladic is being repeatedly mentioned, and he said, "We do need people of authority, but we also have other good commanders." That is literally what he said. "For instance, there's General Krstic. He planned, and I approved those plans for him, the plans for the Srebrenica operation." And he also added, "Of course, the General Staff also assisted, but General Krstic did it." That is what he said. There must be a recording somewhere so that this can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but General Hadzihasanovic, why did you pay so much attention to that statement?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I know General Krstic, and it was a surprise for me. All those events were a surprise for me. Secondly, I knew that he had been Chief of Staff, and then I registered the statement of Mr. Karadzic saying that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand that you were interested, because you were following his career, you were friends, you knew him well. But did that impression stay with you that President Karadzic had named Krstic by means of television? Wouldn't it be necessary to have a paper, a formal decision, a document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression that he was the commander because that is what Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Yes. Another small question for you: Following the documents regarding humanitarian aid that Mr. Harmon showed you, you answered, I think on page 19, line 12 of the LiveNote, you said something like this, and I quote: "And this was confirmed in the document of General Mladic." Do you remember saying that regarding humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because I thought the directive had been read which was signed by General Mladic. Maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the directive of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You also said, and I'm referring to page 27 of the LiveNote, line 20, regarding these reports, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that: "If somebody had provided reliable information or not, I don't know, but I used these documents." Do you -- how do you evaluate the reliability of documents which several subordinates send to the Chief of Staff, for instance? Do you have confidence in that document or are there any reasons that may lead you not to accept it as reliable?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to documents, the organ sending information has a certain number of people who are responsible for those things, and their information is relevant. If that piece of information is being used by somebody writing about the morale of the fighters, they can use that information in various ways - descriptively, this way, or another - so then the information has a different purpose, or for the purpose of information, for instance. But what is sent by operations officers, those are relevant and we consider them to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's a question that has already been asked: Would it be possible that people suffering from hunger could exaggerate the situation to receive humanitarian aid or maybe provide a description that was a faithful description of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the situation such as it was in Srebrenica, it's quite possible that somebody may have added a little or detracted. Anything is possible. I couldn't say with certainty that it is a hundred per cent accurate when it comes to humanitarian aid and the humanitarian situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question by Judge Wald, you spoke about what you heard regarding the executions in Potocari. What did you hear being said by people who arrived as to what they saw and observed of executions in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a detail, when people coming from Srebrenica were referring to an area where the hospital was, that somebody had entered that part of the hospital, mistreating some people there. I don't know whether they killed them. I can't remember exactly. It was a long time ago. But I remember a small wood being mentioned near the UNPROFOR camp where shooting was heard and where people were taken. I remember this being said by the people who were in the compound, the women and the elderly, because I visited, after the fall of Srebrenica, in that time period, the people who were staying in tents near the Tuzla airport. I spoke to them. And then the stories that I heard, I still remember some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what was the physical and mental condition of those people who managed to get through?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HADZIHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is difficult to describe, because they were really ranging from those who were irritable or crying to those who were dumbfounded; they had no words to express their feelings. There were different reactions. But as a whole, they were terrified, they were suffering, they were full of pain and sorrow, because each one of those persons in the tents knew that they had lost someone close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. We have no further questions for you, I think. You have answered our questions, and therefore I thank you very much for coming. I do so on behalf of my colleagues in the Chamber, and I think also on the part of the parties, who had a chance to put questions to you. So we thank you very much and we wish you a safe journey to your country. Thank you very much. I am going to ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a practical matter that needs to be addressed at this point, I think, a number of exhibits which need to be tendered and discussed. I have information that the parties have managed to get together and negotiate, if I may use the word, in order to reach an agreement concerning this issue. So we could perhaps have a 15-minute break at this point so that once again we can organise ourselves, all of us, and then come back to the courtroom and to continue working as long as it is necessary. But I think that there is a limit. I don't think we can work for longer than half an hour at this point. But let me first hear the opinion of the parties, Mr. Harmon first and then later Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are certainly happy for a break, Mr. President. We have had extensive negotiations and discussions on these items. I think we have resolved most of our issues. I would like to, at this time, since the witness has just left, move for the introduction of the exhibits that were introduced by the Prosecutor's office through him and address the remaining exhibits when we come back. The exhibits that I had shown to General Hadzihasanovic were Prosecutor's Exhibits 898 through 904, and I would move for their admission into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you also have exhibits to tender, I assume. Let us hear you on the Prosecution exhibits and also your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not object to any of the exhibits tendered by Mr. Harmon. We should like to tender D179 as Defence exhibit. I also have to express certain reservation regarding the documents that have been offered through the witness that we have just heard, in particular, as regards C2 in respect of which the Defence has managed to establish, despite the brevity of time, that at least two pieces of information contained therein are incorrect and, since the witness did not have the source of the document, we would like to object to the admission of this exhibit since the information sought is precise in nature, but the witness failed to provide adequate explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, your response concerning D179 and also if you wish to say something concerning C2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to D179 being admitted into evidence and we have no comment on C2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber therefore admits into evidence Prosecution exhibits and Defence exhibits that have just been tendered. As for Exhibit C2, the Chamber believes that the witness has authentified [as interpreted] the document and that he has provided adequate explanation to that effect because of the general character of the information sought. So the Chamber admits that document as well whose probative value will be evaluated during the deliberations of the Judges. The same goes for C1 through C5. All of those documents have been admitted. We will have a 15-minute break at this point and come back in order to take stock of the situation regarding exhibits which are still pending and in dispute. --- Break taken at 2.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us resume but with a somewhat different agenda in mind. We have this parcel here that needs to be addressed. We have 30 minutes at our disposal, and we have to see what we can do in those 30 minutes. I think that the most efficient way to proceed would be to hear the parties, who will give us a general idea of what their main concerns are. We will therefore receive information from them first, and then we will come back to discuss the issue or we will decide to make a ruling in writing, depending on what the parties are going to tell us. If you tell us that you have reached an agreement, we will have a sound basis for our decision. If not, we will make a different ruling. So this is just a general idea on how things are as regards the documents that are still pending. Let me first give the floor to Mr. Harmon, and then I will hear the Defence. Is there anything that you can tell us after this break, anything new?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have prepared lists of documents that are outstanding, and we have reached agreements on some and others remain contested. We're prepared to inform Your Honours of which ones are still contested and which ones we have reached agreement on. And I think that's, in response to your question, all I have to say at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Defence? Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have anything to add to what Mr. Harmon has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we therefore hear Mr. Harmon about the results of your talks and a possible agreement? Okay. Mr. Harmon, let us hear you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there should be lists in front of you.
